{"markdown": "Ongoing monitoring evaluates the extent to which this model continues to perform as expected given potential changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data relevance, or market conditions [[reg:SR26-2:V.2]].
The plan below reuses the threshold artifacts already cited by this validation's checks and introduces no new bound.

### Quantities to track and the bound each is tracked against

- Discrimination: recompute AUC on each monitoring window and compare it against the declared floor of 0.7 [[art:8bfd02cc:threshold.package.auc.test.min]], reading the approval-time value of 0.755 [[art:365b7034:metrics.test.auc]] as the reference level rather than as a guarantee of future performance.
- Calibration slope: refit the logistic regression of the realised outcome on logit(p) each window and require the slope to stay within the declared band whose lower bound is 0.8 [[art:95fdb848:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.min]] and whose upper bound is 1.2 [[art:0adb7a89:threshold.package.calibration_slope.test.max]], against the approval-time value of 0.9886 [[art:e06564c7:calibration_slope.test]].
- Calibration error: recompute the Brier score on each window and compare it against the declared ceiling of 0.2 [[art:d0f98b9c:threshold.package.brier.test.max]], noting that this validation records the ceiling but no observed production value.
- Input and score stability: recompute the largest PSI across the scored population, score included, and compare it against the declared ceiling of 0.25 [[art:fbb5a9d1:threshold.package.psi.max]], with the development-time value of 0.003083 [[art:e1d82330:psi.max]] indicating how much headroom existed at approval.
- Realised event rate: track it each window, and when it falls below 0.05 [[art:42f1351e:rule.calibration_first_event_rate]] treat calibration evidence as the leading signal for escalation ahead of discrimination.
- Scoring runtime: track wall-clock time for the scoring run against the declared cap of 300.0 [[art:3f4c6e97:threshold.package.max_seconds]] seconds, since a breach signals an implementation or data-volume change rather than a statistical one.

### Frequency

Stability, event-rate, and runtime measures depend only on inputs and scores and should be produced on the shortest cycle the scoring schedule supports, which for a batch credit model is normally monthly.
Discrimination and calibration measures depend on realised outcomes and should be produced only once a monitoring window has accumulated enough matured defaults to make the estimate meaningful, which for this product is normally quarterly.
The frequency and scope of monitoring reports depend on the nature of the model, the availability of new data or modeling approaches, and model materiality, so the cadence above should be revisited if the model's use or materiality changes [[reg:SR26-2:V.2]].

### Escalation

A measure that crosses its declared bound should trigger investigation rather than automatic action, because a single window can breach for reasons of sample composition alone.
Where performance deviates meaningfully from expectations across consecutive windows, the responsible parties should consider whether overlays, adjustment, recalibration, or redevelopment are warranted [[reg:SR26-2:V.2]].

### What this validation could not cover and monitoring should watch instead

The stability evidence in this report compares development data against the held-out test split, not production data against development data, so genuine population drift after deployment is unobserved here and must be established by the production PSI series.
This validation had no out-of-time sample, so it says nothing about how performance decays with calendar time, and the trend of the quarterly discrimination and calibration series is the only available evidence on that question.
No benchmark model or external comparison was available, and benchmarking against alternative internal or external data or models belongs in the monitoring program, with discrepancies triggering investigation into their sources and degree [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
No override activity exists yet for a model that has not been used in production, so monitoring should record overrides with appropriate documentation and analyse override performance, since a high override rate or overrides that consistently improve outcomes indicates the underlying model needs revision [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
Process verification of the deployed implementation, including that data inputs remain accurate and complete and that code changes are logged and auditable, was outside the scope of this validation and is a standing monitoring obligation [[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]].
Even with sound modeling practices and rigorous validation, material model risk can remain, so users of the output should understand and communicate its limitations and supplement it with complementary analysis [[reg:SR26-2:V]]."}

You are drafting one section of a model-validation report on the model package credit_default version
1.0. The report follows the structure of the Federal Reserve's model risk management
guidance and never claims compliance with it.

Section: ## 7. Ongoing monitoring recommendations

What this section must do:
Recommend ongoing monitoring: which quantities to track, at what frequency, and against which
bound -- citing the same threshold artifacts the checks used rather than inventing new numbers --
and name anything this validation could not cover that monitoring should watch instead.

Rules, all of them checked after you answer:
- Every number you write is followed immediately by its [[art:...]] citation, copied exactly from
  the JSON below. A number with no citation is counted against this report.
- Write no number that is not in the JSON below. If you want to say something the artifacts do not
  support, say it in words without a number.
- One sentence per line. The claim extractor works line by line, so a sentence split over two
  lines is two claims and a paragraph on one line is one.
- For a table artifact, do not retype the cells. Write the directive [[table:<logical_name>]] on a
  line of its own; the renderer expands it, with its caption and its citation, from the store.
- Open the section with a sentence that anchors it to the guidance, carrying one [[reg:...]]
  citation copied from the guidance spans below. Prefer a span of the current guidance, SR26-2;
  cite the superseded SR11-7 only where it says something the revision does not.
- Write markdown. Do not write a level-2 heading: the renderer writes it.
- Do not use the words "compliant" or "certified".

Guidance spans retrieved for this section:
[
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR26-2:V.2]]",
  "heading": "Ongoing Model Monitoring",
  "text": "Ongoing model monitoring involves an evaluation of the extent to which a model is\nperforming as expected given potential changes in products, exposures, activities, clients, data\nrelevance, or market conditions. A model that no longer performs as expected may warrant\noverlays, adjustment, or redevelopment of the model depending on a banking organization\u2019s\nmodel risk management policy as it pertains to model deterioration.\nAn effective ongoing monitoring plan may also include regularly assessing any model\nlimitations at the development stage and over time, along with procedures for responding to any\nissues that may occur, before and after a model is approved for use. The frequency and scope of\nmonitoring reports will depend on the nature of the model, the availability of new data or\nmodeling approaches, and model materiality."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR26-2:V]]",
  "heading": "Model Validation and Monitoring",
  "text": "Model validation evaluates whether models perform as expected and includes an\nassessment of a model\u2019s reliability and its limitations. The nature and rigor of validation generally\nalign with the model\u2019s approach, use, and materiality. Sound validation identifies model\nlimitations and errors and clarifies appropriate use and whether corrective actions may be\nwarranted.\nValidation provides insight into the reliability of a given model, based on its underlying\nassumptions, methods, data, and relevant theories, as appropriate. This understanding helps\ncharacterize the source and extent of the model risk. Validation can reveal performance\ndeterioration over time and inform judgments about acceptable performance ranges. When\nperformance deviates meaningfully from expectations, banking organizations generally consider\nwhether model adjustments, recalibration, or redevelopment are warranted.\nThe timing, nature, and frequency of validation activities vary based on model purpose,\nmodel methodology, frequency and scope of model changes, data limitations, and other practical\nconstraints. Sound practice recognizes that validation approaches may differ across models based\non their characteristics and use. Validation generally occurs prior to a model\u2019s first use.\nHowever, certain circumstances (e.g., an urgent business need) may necessitate using the model\nbefore validation is completed. In those cases, sound practice involves greater attention to the\nmodel\u2019s limitations when considering the appropriateness of its use, informing relevant\nstakeholders of those limitations, and determining appropriate controls (e.g., placing limits on\nmodel use or more closely monitoring its performance).\nThe quality of validation process depends on the rigor and effectiveness of the review\nrather than on organizational structure of the banking organization\u2019s risk management function.\nTechnical knowledge and modeling expertise enable appropriate analysis, meaningful critique,\nand sound judgment about model performance and risk.\nEven with sound modeling practices and rigorous validation, material model risk can\nremain. Users of model output benefit from understanding and communicating limitations,\nmonitoring performance, periodically reviewing relevance, and supplementing model output\nwith complementary analysis and information."
 },
 {
  "citation": "[[reg:SR11-7:V.1.b]]",
  "heading": "Ongoing Monitoring",
  "text": "The second core element of the validation process is ongoing monitoring. Such\nmonitoring confirms that the model is appropriately implemented and is being used and is\nperforming as intended.\nOngoing monitoring is essential to evaluate whether changes in products, exposures,\nactivities, clients, or market conditions necessitate adjustment, redevelopment, or\nreplacement of the model and to verify that any extension of the model beyond its\noriginal scope is valid. Any model limitations identified in the development stage should\nbe regularly assessed over time, as part of ongoing monitoring. Monitoring begins when a\nmodel is first implemented in production systems for actual business use. This\nmonitoring should continue periodically over time, with a frequency appropriate to the\nnature of the model, the availability of new data or modeling approaches, and the\nmagnitude of the risk involved. Banks should design a program of ongoing testing and\nevaluation of model performance along with procedures for responding to any problems\nthat appear. This program should include process verification and benchmarking.\nProcess verification checks that all model components are functioning as designed. It\nincludes verifying that internal and external data inputs continue to be accurate, complete,\nconsistent with model purpose and design, and of the highest quality available. Computer\ncode implementing the model should be subject to rigorous quality and change control\nprocedures to ensure that the code is correct, that it cannot be altered except by approved\nparties, and that all changes are logged and can be audited. System integration can be a\nchallenge and deserves special attention because the model processing component often\ndraws from various sources of data, processes large amounts of data, and then feeds into\nmultiple data repositories and reporting systems. User-developed applications, such as\nspreadsheets or ad hoc database applications used to generate quantitative estimates, are\nparticularly prone to model risk. As the content or composition of information changes\nover time, systems may need to be updated to reflect any changes in the data or its use.\nReports derived from model outputs should be reviewed as part of validation to verify\nthat they are accurate, complete, and informative, and that they contain appropriate\nindicators of model performance and limitations.\nMany of the tests employed as part of model development should be included in ongoing\nmonitoring and be conducted on a regular basis to incorporate additional information as it\nbecomes available. New empirical evidence or theoretical research may suggest the need\nto modify or even replace original methods. Analysis of the integrity and applicability of [Page Break]\ninternal and external information sources, including information provided by third-party\nvendors, should be performed regularly.\nSensitivity analysis and other checks for robustness and stability should likewise be\nrepeated periodically. They can be as useful during ongoing monitoring as they are\nduring model development. If models only work well for certain ranges of input values,\nmarket conditions, or other factors, they should be monitored to identify situations where\nthese constraints are approached or exceeded.\nOngoing monitoring should include the analysis of overrides with appropriate\ndocumentation. In the use of virtually any model, there will be cases where model output\nis ignored, altered, or reversed based on the expert judgment of model users. Such\noverrides are an indication that, in some respect, the model is not performing as intended\nor has limitations. Banks should evaluate the reasons for overrides and track and analyze\noverride performance. If the rate of overrides is high, or if the override process\nconsistently improves model performance, it is often a sign that the underlying model\nneeds revision or redevelopment.\nBenchmarking is the comparison of a given model's inputs and outputs to estimates from\nalternative internal or external data or models. It can be incorporated in model\ndevelopment as well as in ongoing monitoring. For credit risk models, examples of\nbenchmarks include models from vendor firms or industry consortia and data from retail\ncredit bureaus. Pricing models for securities and derivatives often can be compared with\nalternative models that are more accurate or comprehensive but also too time consuming\nto run on a daily basis. Whatever the source, benchmark models should be rigorous and\nbenchmark data should be accurate and complete to ensure a reasonable comparison.\nDiscrepancies between the model output and benchmarks should trigger investigation\ninto the sources and degree of the differences, and examination of whether they are\nwithin an expected or appropriate range given the nature of the comparison. The results\nof that analysis may suggest revisions to the model. However, differences do not\nnecessarily indicate that the model is in error. The benchmark itself is an alternative\nprediction, and the differences may be due to the different data or methods used. If the\nmodel and the benchmark match well, that is evidence in favor of the model, but it should\nbe interpreted with caution so the bank does not get a false degree of comfort."
 }
]
